Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

Arrowheads depict the pericardium.
case_info.explanation: C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

Case:
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Image Explanation:
A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Cardiac catheterization
  B. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
  C. Computed tomography of the chest
  D. Transesophageal echocardiography

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

turn_prompts.response:
Based on the imaging and exam findings, I suspect the chest pressure and echo abnormalities are secondary to pectus excavatum rather than true constrictive pericarditis, especially given the normal JVP and absence of classic Doppler signs like mitral inflow variation. The most appropriate next step is to obtain cardiac MRI to definitively assess pericardial anatomy and ventricular interaction while also evaluating the impact of the chest wall deformity.

<belief>C</belief>

A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

Image Explanation:
Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Recommend avoiding heavy lifting, initiate β-blocker therapy, and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week
  B. Obtain blood cultures, begin empiric antibiotics, and admit with telemetry
  C. Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements, perform a triple rule-out chest computed tomographic angiogram, and admit to observation
  D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

turn_prompts.response:
Based on the findings of a new grade 6 diastolic murmur, thrill, and ECG evidence of LV hypertrophy suggesting acute aortic regurgitation, the most appropriate next step is urgent echocardiography to assess valve morphology, regurgitation severity, and ventricular function. This is a potentially unstable hemodynamic emergency that requires immediate diagnostic confirmation in the ED.

<belief>D</belief>

Case:
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

Image Explanation:
Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

turn_prompts.response:
The patient’s severe mitral regurgitation and dyspnea are clearly linked to the onset of LBBB, resolving when QRS narrows at rest, pointing to a mechanically induced valvular dysfunction driven by dyssynchrony. Since exercise reproduces both LBBB and severe MR with symptoms, restoring coordinated contraction is the physiologic priority. The most appropriate step is cardiac resynchronization to correct the underlying dyssynchrony and prevent recurrent functional MR.

<belief>B</belief>

case_info.explanation: C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. case_info.explanation: C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

case_info.explanation: C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

messages.content:
You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A man in his early 50s presented with recurrent episodes of cough, palpitations, shortness of breath, and exertional chest pain. He had a history of type 2 diabetes but had no history of smoking or other cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. There was no family history of sudden cardiac death. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an ST-segment elevation in leads V1and V2(Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a right lung mass, and coronary CT angiography indicated stenosis in the right coronary and left anterior descending coronary arteries.

[Clinician's statement]
We have established a clear and stable consensus on the management priority.

[AI assistant's reply]
Agreed. Our consensus on performing emergency coronary angiography as the next step ensures we are managing the patient's highest immediate risk appropriately.

[Case Scenario]
A woman aged in her late 20s presented for follow-up regarding her chest pain. Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

[Management Options]
  A. Continue current therapy with tapering after improvement in markers and cardiac MRI
  B. Initiate IL-1ras for shorter than recommended duration with current therapy wean
  C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean
  D. Surgical pericardiectomy
